title: Claim first
prompt: Write one paragraph whose first sentence could stand alone as your whole argument. Every following sentence must earn its place by supporting, complicating, or qualifying that first one.

title: Argue, then concede
prompt: Take the claim 'AI tutoring flattens pedagogy.' Write one paragraph that argues it, then one that concedes the strongest objection without collapsing.

title: Dig up the claim
prompt: Find a paragraph you wrote in the last year (an email, a report, a post). Without looking at it again, write the paragraph you meant: claim in the first sentence, context only where the reader needs it.

title: Thesis in twelve words
prompt: Write the thesis of an essay you'd like to write in twelve words or fewer. Then write three sentences, each the first sentence of a paragraph that would support it.

title: Find the turn
prompt: Write a short essay in three paragraphs: what most people believe about something you know well, the moment that belief stopped working for you, and what you believe now. The second paragraph is the turn; make the reader feel it.

title: Explain it to one person
prompt: Explain a concept from your field to one specific, named person who is intelligent but outside it. Use one concrete example and no jargon you haven't earned by defining it.

title: Down the ladder
prompt: Pick an abstract word you use at work (alignment, engagement, scaffolding, impact). Write a paragraph that never uses it but makes the reader see exactly what you mean by it.

title: Periodic and loose
prompt: Write the same idea twice: once as a periodic sentence that holds its main clause to the end, once as a loose sentence that leads with it and accumulates. Then write two sentences on which one this idea wants.

title: No hedges
prompt: Write a paragraph arguing something you believe about teaching or learning, with no hedges: no 'perhaps', 'arguably', 'somewhat', 'it could be said', 'I think'. Qualify only where the evidence requires it, and say exactly how.

title: A post you'd sign
prompt: Write a LinkedIn post about something you noticed this week at work. No hook formulas, no lists of lessons, no 'Here's the thing.' One observation, one claim, one honest line about what you don't know yet.

title: Open a unit
prompt: Write the opening paragraph of a course unit, addressed to the learner. Say what they will be able to do by the end and why it matters to them, without the words 'learn', 'understand', or 'explore'.

title: Steelman
prompt: State the strongest version of a view you disagree with so well that someone who holds it would sign it. Don't rebut it. Stop when you've made it as strong as it can be.

title: One fact, fully used
prompt: Take one fact, statistic or observed incident and build a paragraph around it: what it is, why it's surprising, what it does and doesn't prove. Resist adding a second fact.

title: Aphorisms
prompt: Write five one-sentence aphorisms about writing, in the manner of Emerson or La Rochefoucauld. Each should be quotable, slightly unfair, and true enough to sting.

title: A scene inside an essay
prompt: Write the opening of an essay that starts with a single scene — one moment, one place, a few lines of what was said — and then, in the second paragraph, steps back to say what the scene is evidence of.

title: Paragraph architecture
prompt: Write a paragraph that moves from general to specific, then one on the same subject that moves from specific to general. Note in a line which serves the reader better here.

title: Land it
prompt: Write the last paragraph of an essay about why you stopped writing for yourself. It must not summarise. End on an image, an action, or a question the essay has earned.

title: What they notice
prompt: Write a 150-word paragraph in which a character enters a room and we learn something about them only through what they notice. No adjectives describing the character.

title: Scene, then summary
prompt: Write a year of a marriage in one paragraph of summary, then one evening of it in full scene. Choose the evening the summary was hiding.

title: Subtext
prompt: Two people discuss what to have for dinner. Neither says it, but one of them has decided to leave. Dialogue only, with no more than three lines of action.

title: Free indirect
prompt: Write a paragraph in close third person that slips into the character's idiom without quotation marks or 'she thought'. The reader should hear the character's words inside the narrator's sentences.

title: Zoom
prompt: Write five sentences that move steadily from far to near psychic distance (Gardner's ladder): from 'It was winter of the year 1853' to the inside of one person's head.

title: The object carries it
prompt: Write a scene in which an object is handed from one person to another, and the whole emotional weight of their relationship is in how it's handed over. Don't name an emotion.

title: A voice not yours
prompt: Write a monologue in the first person by someone whose politics, age and vocabulary differ sharply from yours, explaining why they did something they're a little ashamed of. Let them be persuasive.

title: Opening lines
prompt: Write five possible first sentences for the same story. Each must establish a different thing first: voice, situation, character, place, or a question. Mark the one you'd keep.

title: Gesture, not adverb
prompt: Write an argument between a parent and a child of eight using only 'said' as a tag and no adverbs. Let gesture and rhythm carry the tone.

title: White space
prompt: Write two short sections separated by a line break and ten years. The second section should make the reader reinterpret something in the first.

title: Weather as character
prompt: Describe a street at the moment before something happens. The reader should feel what's coming without being told. Use no more than two adjectives.

title: The narrator is wrong
prompt: Write a first-person paragraph in which the narrator explains why a colleague dislikes them. The reader should understand the real reason before the narrator does.

title: End on the image
prompt: Write the last paragraph of a story about a reconciliation that doesn't quite happen. End on a physical image, not a realisation.

title: What does the dragon sound like?
prompt: Write what a dragon says when it's scared, and what it says when it's trying to look brave. Make them sound different!

title: Five senses door
prompt: You open a door in your house that wasn't there yesterday. Write what you see, hear, smell, feel, and taste.
